beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: Nothing new. This is the title of the module.

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: Nothing new. It reads like a consultant's disclaimer slide.

beats.trigger: **Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.**
beats.got: I need an example of a tool people got and didn't use. I have one, the BI dashboard rollout.

beats.trigger: **Test** the switch assumptions and name one person and one test to take out of the room
beats.got: The module is about interviewing a teammate, choosing what to share, and planning it. It's closer to my problem than prompt tips would be.

beats.trigger: Industry analysts expect agent adoption to accelerate significantly over the coming years.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's an analyst line with no source, and I'd cut it from my own deck.

beats.trigger: What decides whether sharing works is **the job** your teammate is trying to get done.
beats.got: Start from the teammate's job, not from my stuff. Jobs-to-be-done is familiar from consulting, but it's the right frame for this.

beats.trigger: If it could describe anyone in the room, point to the generic line and ask the agent to try that part again.
beats.got: The agent reads my working files and drafts the teammate's job, and I check it for specifics. That's a useful test. I'd do it with the pricing working group.

beats.trigger: Clear communication, strong sponsorship and regular follow-up remain the foundation
beats.got: Nothing new. I've read this paragraph twice already.

beats.trigger: finds what would stop that candidate from being absorbed and turns it into a technical plan plus a people plan.
beats.got: This is a pointer to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: Find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: One obstacle, two plans. That's clear, and it's what I came for.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Don't pick the first technical limit. Cluster the obstacles and name the one that explains the others. That's a quality test I can use.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: My plans always look better on the tech side. Unnamed owners in the people plan is the thing to catch, and it hits my team's situation.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: Another pointer. The next exercise ends in a Monday file.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are hypotheses to test, not deliverables. I agree.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: I ask what must be true for them to drop their current way of working, and pick two or three tests for this week. It's a sharp question, and it fits my pricing-pilot rollout.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: The agent writes three failure stories and I carry the strongest into a Monday move: one person, one question, one test. That's concrete enough to do.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping. A candidate picked because it moves the outcome is design.
beats.got: Pick by outcome, not by what fits the stack. This is what I'd repeat to my team.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: Nothing new. This is the lecture title, and it names the problem I recognise.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute. Absorption happens in other people's weeks, at their pace, for their reasons.
beats.got: Access and absorption are different things and get reported as one number. My licence-count dashboard does exactly that.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: A good analysis can die because leadership didn't own it, and trust in the people who did the work decides what happens next. That's my CFO and the pricing pilot. It's also a bit long and a bit portentous at the end.

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: Nothing new. This is the third time I've read this paragraph.

beats.trigger: the ones that start early will be best placed.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's the same unsourced analyst claim, and it makes me trust the rest a little less.

beats.trigger: Not *how do I get them to adopt this?* but *what would have to be true for them to switch?*
beats.got: Flip the question. Instead of pushing adoption, ask what has to be true for them to switch. The answers are small and specific, like where they already look and who used it first.

beats.trigger: Have the conversation before you build anything more.
beats.got: Talk to one person before building more. Their answer tells me which plan to keep.

beats.trigger: agents are simply one more area where those principles apply.
beats.got: Nothing new. I skipped it.

beats.trigger: This is a rapidly evolving area, and organisations of every size are working out how best to approach it.
beats.got: Nothing new. If this is the fourth repeat, someone pasted it in by accident.

beats.trigger: Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.
beats.got: I bring the monday file and what the person said. I like that the answer counts as evidence and the plan stays a hypothesis.

beats.trigger: ## Next
beats.got: Nothing new. The heading is empty.

take_homes: Access isn't absorption. Counting who has the tool says nothing about whether they use it, so I should interview the teammate about their job first and not start from what I built.
Write the technical plan and the people plan together. If the people plan has unnamed roles, that is the finding.
Ask what would have to be true for them to switch from their current way of working, then test two or three of those assumptions with one named person.

monday.move: Talk to one pricing working group member (Mika, who owns the pilot-cohort numbers) about how they build the brief today. Ask which source they open first and what they'd need to see before dropping their spreadsheet. Then pick one assumption and test it with the next brief.
monday.who: Mika from the pricing working group
monday.when: Monday morning, 20 minutes before the working group sync
monday.stop_condition: Mika says they already get what they need from the spreadsheet and would not switch. Then I drop this candidate and rethink what I'm offering.
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the context files and everyone keeps their own copy. The people plan names the owner but not where the files live.

misconception.why: I came in thinking the skill was better prompts. This module put the work in who picks it up, where it sits and who vouches for it. I still think a good prompt matters, but it's not what stops fourteen people from running private experiments.

one_line: The core idea, that access isn't absorption and you start by interviewing one person about their job, is good and I'd use it. But four copies of the same context-note filler made me stop trusting the slide deck.
